Distance distribution plots show that Glu136 and Gly340 maintain a hydrogen bond across the three conformational states, whereas Glu136 and Glu508 side-chain distances are more likely to increase as SERT transitions to the IF state (Fig. S28 A and B ). As a result, the number of water molecules within this region increases, thus rearranging the hydrogen bonding network to enable transitions of TM6 for substrate release (Figs. 3 A , B , and S28 C). To observe how Glu508 protonation affects the structural fold of this region, we simulated SERT with Glu508 in its deprotonated form. As anticipated, the negative charges from opposing glutamate residues repel one another and expand this buried pocket (Fig. S28 B ). Interestingly, in some simulations, the Na þ ion from the Na1 site migrates to this cavity where it is then coordinated by the carboxylates of Glu136 and Glu508 and the sulfur of Met135 through water molecules (Fig. 3 C ). A third metal ion site (the Na3 site, to be consistent with prior nomenclature) has not previously been described in SERT, but computational modeling, biochemical analysis, and electrophysiology recordings indicate that equivalent residues of the neuronal glycine transporter 2 (GlyT2) have been suggested to form this third Na þ site (98,99). The substrate translocation process of SERT Using transition path theory, the highest flux pathway for conformational change and 5-HT import can be determined from the MSM and used to predict an ordered sequence of binding events and structural changes. SERT undergoes complete transitions to the IF state in the simulations, with permeation toward the intracellular side upon binding of substrates in the order following Na þ , 5-HT, and Cl À ions (Fig. 4 ). We describe each step of the import process in detail. The import process begins with the binding of Na þ to the Na1 site, followed by a second Na þ binding the Na2 site (Figs. S29 and S30 ). These two sites are well described in the SERT crystal structure and the literature (23, 45, 47, 100) . Na þ bound at the Na1 site couples activity between the ion and substrate binding sites, whereas computational studies of related transporters have indicated that Na þ coordinated at the Na2 site dissociates during the transporter cycle to become the symported metal ion (40, 101, 102) . The importance of the Na2 site is underscored by its conservation in distantly related secondary transporters (103). Na þ ions entering the transporter interact with Asp328 and Asn112 at the extracellular surface, then rapidly diffuse into the allosteric site (Figs. S29 A and S30 A). Here, the Na þ ions interact with Glu493 and Glu494, and a rotameric shift in Glu493 enables the ions to descend past the extracellular gate to their central binding sites (Figs. S29 B , C, S30 B, and C). Na1 is stabilized by Ala96, Asn101, Ser336, and Asn368 (Fig. S29 D), while Na2 is coordinated by backbone carbonyls of Gly94, Val97, Leu434, and side chains of Asp437 and Ser438 (Fig. S30 D ). Previous simulations of SERT have shown Asp437 as a key residue for maintaining Na2-ion interactions (102), and mutations of Asp437 and Ser438 have confirmed their role in coordination and dissociation of Na2 (102, 104) . Similar to other transporters in the NSS family (29,83,84), the binding of Na þ ions to their respective sites stabilizes SERT in the OF state while neutralizing the polar cavity to allow protonated 5-HT diffusion. 5-HT is recognized by Tyr107, Ile108, Gln111, and Asp328 at the extracellular vestibule to initiate the binding in the OF state. Ile108 forms hydrophobic contacts with the indole ring of 5-HT, while other residues form polar interactions with the substrate that favors binding. 5-HT then diffuses inside the translocation pore and binds to the allosteric site (Fig. 5 B ). The substrate is stabilized by aromatic ring packing against Phe335 and Arg104, and a hydrogen bonding network with Asp328, Gln332, and Glu494 (Fig. 5 B ). The antidepressant molecule vilazodone binds to the allosteric site where it forms similar aromatic interactions to the endogenous substrate (105) (Fig. S31 A ). Furthermore, previous mutations of residues in the allosteric site have been shown to alter inhibitor potency (106) . 5-HT undergoes a 90 rotation by rapidly exchanging its polar interactions and shifts toward the orthosteric site (Fig. 5C ). The switching of amine group interactions to Glu494 triggers the movement of 5-HT from the allosteric site to the orthosteric site. 5-HT rotates such that the conformation becomes perpendicular to the membrane, which is further favored by polar and hydrophobic interactions by Asp328, Gln332, Leu502, and Ala331. The extracellular gating residues form a salt bridge interaction and enlarge the binding cavity such that substrate can escape to the primary binding site. This substrate binding site in the NSS family contains three well-studied subsites and has served as the basis for designing various tricyclic antidepressant molecules (107) . In the orthosteric site, the indole moiety forms aromatic interactions with Tyr95 and Phe341, while the protonated amine moiety of 5-HT interacts with Asp98 of subsite A, disrupting the hydrogen bond between Asp98 and Tyr176 (Fig. S32 ). Tyr176 is highly conserved among the SLC6 family, whereas Asp98 is uniquely conserved in only monoamine transporters; the majority of SLC6 transporters contain glycine in this position.

llm_chunks.text: The permeation of the Cl À into the extracellular vestibule is accompanied by an additional extracellular Na þ ion. As the ions approach the extracellular gating residues, the Na þ ion disrupts the salt bridge by interacting with Glu493 and Glu494 to allow Cl À to form polar interactions with Arg104 and Tyr176. The shift of the guanidinium group of Arg104 then facilitates the diffusion of the Cl À ion into the central cavity (Fig. S33 B ). The accompanying Na þ ion then diffuses out to the extracellular space as the orthosteric cavity is neutralized by the substrate and Na þ ions in the Na1 and Na2 site. Interestingly, we observed the binding of the Cl À ion to occur solely in 5-HT-SERT simulations. Despite Cl À ions being present in the solvent of Na þ -SERT simulations, we only observe the binding of Na þ ions to the transporter within the simulated timescales (Fig. S34 ). To further investigate this phenomenon, we calculated the electrostatic potential using the adaptive Poisson-Boltzmann solver (APBS) (114) . Projection of the electrostatic potential of the SERT three-dimensional structure shows that the extracellular vestibule of SERT is highly electronegative and remains electronegative after the bind-ing of the two Na þ ions, as observed in Na þ -SERT simulations (Fig. S35 A and B ). When 5-HT is bound in the orthosteric site, the extracellular vestibule is then neutralized to allow for favorable diffusion of Cl À . The additional interaction of Cl À with the indole-NH of 5-HT further stabilizes the ion in the exposed extracellular recognition site (Fig. 5 D ). The indole ring of 5-HT occupies subsite C of the primary binding site, which in turn favors the transition of the Cl À ion to its binding site (Fig. S31 B ). The simulated Na1, Na2, and Cl À sites concur with their respective sites observed in crystal structures of SERT, LeuT, and DAT (23,45,47,100) (Fig. S36 ). The binding of ions and the substrate to their respective sites leads to the closure of the extracellular gates to obtain the OC state where the permeation pathway is closed at both ends. The decrease of the pore results in shifting the aromatic ring of 5-HT from subsite C to subsite B within the orthosteric binding pocket. The amine moiety of the neurotransmitter remains bound to Asp98, Tyr95, and the C-terminal pole of TM1a within subsite A (Fig. 6 A and B ). The simulated configuration of 5-HT in subsite B agrees with the crystal structure of dopamine-bound dDAT (100) (Fig. S36 F ). The indole-NH ring of 5-HT interacts with Thr473 and other hydrophobic contacts by Ala169, Ala441, Gly442, and Leu443 residues stabilizing the substrate in subsite B. Additionally, 5-HT may enter into subsite B in which the indole-NH is oriented toward Phe341 adopting a binding pose also reported in previous modeling studies (110, 115) . Previous experimental studies indicate that mutations of these residues can decrease 5-HT transport (106,111), and the binding pose is further supported by several studies showing that interactions in subsite B are critical for inhibitor potency (107, 111, 112) .

Na þ loses its interaction with the backbone carbonyl of Leu434 and enters the intracellular vestibule, thereby initiating structural transitions from the OC to IF state. Koldsø et al. have shown that solvation of the intracellular vestibule allows Asp437 to rotate Na2 toward the intracellular pathway and facilitates transitions to the IF conformation (102) . Similarly, we also observed that the rotameric shift in Asp437 initiates the dissociation of Na þ from the Na2 site (Fig. S37 A and B ). The Na þ ion then interacts with Ser91 and is further stabilized by Phe347 and Phe440 via cation-p interactions (Fig. S37 C ). Furthermore, as the intracellular pathway is formed, the interactions of TM1a and TM8 that coordinate the Na2 site are decoupled, further facilitating the outward motion of TM1a from TM5 and TM8. However, in Na þ -SERT simulations, the Na2 ion has a tendency to rebind to the Na2 site after release (Fig. S38 ). Such intracellular binding events were not observed in 5-HT-SERT simulations. The coupling of 5-HT import to the cytoplasmic release of Na þ from the Na2 site explains the 1:1 sodium to neurotransmitter stoichiometry of the transport cycle. llm_chunks.heading: CONCLUSIONS
llm_chunks.text: In this study, we present an atomistic view of the substrate import process in SERT as well as characterizing the thermodynamics of key states involved in substrate transport. By implementing an MSM-based adaptive sampling protocol to sample the conformational landscape, we investigated global transitions from OF to IF for both 5-HT-free and 5-HT-importing SERT. MSM-weighted conformational free energy landscapes show the OF and OC states are relatively stable, and transitions to and from OF and OC states are relatively low energy. Transitions from OC to IF are substantially higher, with energy barriers of $3 kcal/mol in Na þ -SERT; however, the presence of 5-HT not only lowers the free energy barrier of OF to OC transitions but further stabilizes SERT in the IF state compared with SERT in the absence of 5-HT. The dependence of the IF state on the presence of substrate has experimentally been observed for the bacterial LeuT transporter, where addition of extracellular substrate promotes dynamics at the intracellular gate (82) . The simulated structures show similar helix orientations at the extracellular and intracellular gates with respect to experimental SERT structures (23, 45, 47) . The comparison of Na þ and 5-HT-SERT data reveal that the structural transitions from OF to OC involve minimal helix movements in TM1b, TM6a, and TM10, while OC to IF transitions show higher fluctuations of intracellular helix tips of TM1a, TM5, and TM7 to facilitate opening of the intracellular vestibule (Fig. S22 ). Biochemical experiments in conjunction with computational modeling have shown that cholesterol binding to a conserved site comprising TM1a, TM5, and TM7 inhibits these helix movements and may act as a regulatory mechanism for SERT function (47, 117, 118) . Deviations were observed in the opening of the intracellular vestibule of the IF state between the cryo-EM and predicted MD structures, specifically the outward motion of TM1a. As such, the observed exit pathway is lined between TM1a and TM5, as opposed to an alternative pathway between TM1a and TM6b as proposed based on resolved IF structures (23, 51, 116) . This might reflect the loss of lateral pressure following detergent extraction; the membrane is anticipated to constrain the extent to which TM1a can move away from the helical bundle. Nevertheless, our results show that partial opening of the intracellular pathway is sufficient for substrate transport. Experimental studies of LeuT also indicate that a partially open IF conformation is suitable for substrate transport (28) . Conducting simulations of both serotonin-free and serotonin-present conditions allows us to examine the finer details of the substrate-induced conformational transitions and the cooperative nature between the transporter and the substrate. Motions of TM2 were highly correlated with TM1b in Na þ -SERT, whereas the binding of 5-HT decreases the cooperativity as TM1b rotates and closes the extracellular cavity to open the exit pathway (Fig. 7 A ). The conformation dynamics examined through HDX studies reveal that TM2 undergoes less fluctuation when bound to Na þ , in contrast to when the transporter is substrate bound (56) . Similar trends were observed between TM6a and TM2; more specifically, the presence of 5-HT destabilizes this region and favors the conformational change required for substrate transport (Fig. 7 A) . Gating residues Arg104-Glu493 remain open until the ions and 5-HT bind to the primary binding site, and later close the extracellular cavity as the exit pathway opens to allow the release of substrate molecules (Fig. S16 ). At the binding site, Tyr176 has the tendency to form a polar interaction with Asp98 in the OF and OC states. Interactions by the amine moiety of the substrate sever the Tyr176-Asp98 interaction, which is further disrupted when the opening of the intracellular cavity induces a rotameric shift in Tyr176 away from Asp98 (Fig. S32 ). Most significantly, the closure of the extracellular allosteric cavity is coupled to opening of the intracellular helix TM1a when serotonin is bound (Fig. 7 C ). Experimental studies show that the substrate binding increases dynamics between EL4 and TM12 (24, (56) (57) (58) . In simulations, EL4 inserts deep inside the extracellular cavity, which is further facilitated by the movement of TM12 (Fig. S39 ). Furthermore, HDX studies on DAT support the coupled motions between TM7 and TM12 observed in simulations when the substrate is bound, compared with just Na þ binding (Fig. 7 A ). Our simulations show an ordered sequence of binding and transport events that agree with the 1:1 substrate:Na þ stoichiometry as previously characterized for the NSS family. First, Na þ ions favorably bind to the Na1 and Na2 sites, followed by 5-HT and Cl À ion to their respective binding sites. The binding of ions and the substrate triggers the closure of the extracellular permeation pathway and subsequent opening of the intracellular gating helices. Finally, the release of Na þ from the Na2 site decouples the interactions between TM1a, TM5, and TM8, increasing the solvation of the intracellular permeation pathway and allowing TM1a to open for substrate release. As unbiased MD simulations sample events with low free energy barriers, we have the highest likelihood of observing the most probable binding sequence of ions and substrate. However, we do not disregard that different sequences of ion and substrate binding events with higher associated free energy barriers are possible and may alter the kinetics of the SERT transport cycle. For example, as both Na þ and Cl À ions were present in the solution in Na þ -SERT simulations, we observed the rapid diffusion and binding of Na þ ions to their binding sites instead of Cl À ion binding (Fig. S34 ).

llm_chunks.heading: CONCLUSIONS
llm_chunks.text: nergy barriers are possible and may alter the kinetics of the SERT transport cycle. For example, as both Na þ and Cl À ions were present in the solution in Na þ -SERT simulations, we observed the rapid diffusion and binding of Na þ ions to their binding sites instead of Cl À ion binding (Fig. S34 ). Simulations conducted by Szo ¨ll} osi and Stockner showed how, if Cl À is initially bound to SERT, a stronger negative electrostatic potential is generated to allow more favorable Na þ binding compared with a completely apo transporter (119). From 5-HT-SERT simulations, Cl À entering the transporter is enabled by Na þ ions breaking the ionic interactions between Arg104 and Glu493 and further facilitated by the substrate in the orthosteric cavity. While the binding of 5-HT neutralizes the electronegative binding cavity, Cl À binding may be possible without the substrate but with higher free energy barriers. A recent study has shown that binding of Na þ and Cl À alone can trigger the closure of the extracellular pathway in the glycine transporter GlyT1b (120) . Projection of the electrostatic potential of hGlyT1b shows the extracellular vestibule to be closer to neutral than hSERT, which may favor Cl À binding without the substrate (Fig. S40 ). Recent discussions regarding the role of the Cl À ion in SERT suggest that Cl À is not released into the intracellular space but remains bound to the transporter (121, 122) . Although SERT is capable of transporting 5-HT without Cl À present, the uptake rates are heavily diminished (123), possibly alluding to higher free energy barriers. Thus, Cl À could be considered a requirement to facilitate necessary substrate-ion coupling for substrate translocation. Nevertheless, the role of the Cl À ion and its implications on the stoichiometry, electroneutrality, ion-substrate coupling, and conformational dynamics highlight discrepancies in the current understanding of substrate transport in the NSS family. This study has explored the conformational dynamics and substrate import of a monomeric unit of SERT; however, fluorescent microscopy has shown SERT to form functional oligomers in the membrane (124, 125) . The LeuT crystal structure has been resolved as a dimeric unit, and while recent modeling studies have explored possible dimeric SERT units (126), the exact interface of SERT FIGURE 7 Cross-correlation analysis of Na þ -SERT and 5-HT-SERT simulations. The set of simulations conducted in this study were initiated from the SERT crystal structure without the full-length N and C termini. Indeed, the cytoplasmic terminal domains are important elements of the NSS structure. Notably, protein-protein interactions of the SNARE protein syntaxin 1A and the N terminus are involved in regulating surface expression, transport activity, membrane trafficking, and phosphorylation of various NSS transporters (14, (127) (128) (129) (130) . In hDAT, phosphatidylinositol 4,5-biphosphate (PIP2) directly interacts with the N terminus to induce inward open conformations (54, 131) . Not only are the terminal residues highly diverse in sequence and length across the entire human NSS family but the lack of structural data of the termini presents inherent challenges to accurately initialize and validate a full-length SERT structural model. Nevertheless, Fenollar-Ferrer et al. combined de novo modeling with biophysical and spectroscopic techniques to provide initial insights into how the SERT N and C termini may structurally influence the conformational cycle and regulatory interaction partners (132). While truncation of the N-terminal residues retains serotonin transport function (133), the transport kinetics may be altered and therefore the rates calculated by the MSM may not represent exact in vivo conditions. Further investigation is required into understanding how in vivo regulation further affects the kinetics and conformational landscape of SERT.

However, the neural mechanisms of stress resilience and its relevance to antidepressant actions remain elusive. In rodents, chronic stress induces dendritic atrophy and decreases dendritic spine density in the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC), recapitulating prefrontal alterations in depressive patients, and the mPFC promotes stress resilience. Whereas dopamine neurons projecting to the nucleus accumbens potentiated by chronic stress promote stress susceptibility, dopamine neurons projecting to the mPFC activated upon acute stress contribute to dendritic growth of mPFC neurons via dopamine D1 receptors, leading to stress resilience. llm_chunks.heading: Introduction
llm_chunks.text: Aversive physical and psychological stimuli perturb the homeostasis of our bodies and evoke common biological responses, including autonomic, neuroendocrine, and behavioral responses, regardless of the type of stimulus (Szabo et al., 2012) . The term "stress" was coined to represent these non-specific responses of the body to any demand for changes (Selye, 1950) . However, there are profound individual differences in the consequences of stress. In some individuals, stressful stimuli induce harmful responses, including behavioral and physiological abnormalities. The impact of stress on health often becomes more serious, precipitating the onset and relapse of symptoms in a range of psychiatric illnesses, including major depressive disorder (MDD), post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), and relapse to drug-seeking. Therefore, the vast amount of work in this field has focused on investigating how stress alters brain function related to psychiatric illnesses (McEwen et al., 2016) . However, the same stressful stimuli have no discernible deleterious effect and do not cause psychiatric illnesses in many others (Franklin et al., 2012; Russo et al., 2012) . This observation of individual differences in stress reactivity has led to the concept of resilience. According to the American Psychological Association, resilience is defined as "the process of adapting well in the face of adversity, trauma, tragedy, threats, or significant source of stress" (Anon, 2014) . Unique characteristics of resilient individuals have received substantial attention in the last decade, and growing efforts in animal models have attempted to unravel the neural and molecular mechanisms of resilience (Cathomas et al., 2019; Furuyashiki and Kitaoka, 2019; Russo et al., 2012) . These animal studies have identified the roles of several molecules and neural circuits across multiple brain regions, including the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) and other limbic and midbrain structures (Akil et al., 2018; Bhatnagar, 2021) . Although some molecular and cellular mechanisms identified in resilience are opposite to those of stress susceptibility, others play unique roles in stress resilience (Cathomas et al., 2019) . This fact suggests that resilience is not merely due to the absence of maladaptive responses to stress but rather active and adaptive processes to counteract stress. Recent clinical studies have shown that low-dose ketamine relieves depressive symptoms within hours, and it has been approved to treat treatment-resistant depression and suicidal ideation. Low-dose ketamine treatment prior to chronic stress exposure reportedly protects animals from developing depressive behaviors (Brachman et al., 2016; McGowan et al., 2018) , suggesting that it augments stress resilience. Recent preclinical studies revealed molecular and neural-circuit mechanisms for its behavioral effects, which overlap with those of stress resilience via the prefrontal dopaminergic system (Duman et al., 2019b; Shinohara et al., 2021) , corroborating the relationship between stress resilience and the actions of low-dose ketamine. Thus, neurobiological studies of stress resilience and low-dose ketamine may be instrumental for each other, and the mechanistic understanding of stress resilience may be exploitable for developing antidepressants based on a naturally occurring mechanism, thus safer than low-dose ketamine. In this review article, we will discuss a possible mechanistic link between stress resilience and the antidepressant actions of low-dose ketamine by summarizing recent preclinical research on each of these phenomena, focusing on the roles of the mPFC that is vulnerable to stress and affected in many psychiatric illnesses (Arnsten, 2015; Davidson and McEwen, 2012; Hare and Duman, 2020) .

llm_chunks.heading: Prefrontal alterations in MDD patients and animal models and their relevance to stress resilience
llm_chunks.text: A large body of postmortem and brain imaging studies of MDD patients have reported reductions in grey-matter volume in the prefrontal cortex, and this decrease correlates with the length of illness (Belleau et al., 2019; Drevets, 2001; Harrison, 2002; Sheline, 2003) . Reduced synaptic markers and the number of synapses in the prefrontal cortex have been reported in postmortem studies of MDD subjects (Kang et al., 2012) . A recent positron emission tomography study shows decreased levels of ligand binding to synaptic vesicle glycoprotein 2A (SV2A) in the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, anterior cingulate cortex, and hippocampus of MDD patients in a manner correlated with depression severity (Holmes et al., 2019) , providing evidence of reduced synapse number in these brain regions. Brain imaging studies of MDD patients have reported altered activity in multiple cerebral cortices (Duman et al., 2019a) . It was reported that deep brain stimulation applied to white matter tracts adjacent to the subgenual cingulate gyrus produced a sustained remission of depressive symptoms in treatment-resistant depressive patients who failed to respond to several standard treatments (Mayberg et al., 2005) . These results support the hypothesis that altered functional activity in the prefrontal cortex is responsible for key symptoms of depression. Animal models provide further evidence for structural changes. Our group and others have used chronic social defeat stress (i.e., repeated exposure to social defeat stress) model to segregate susceptible and resilient subpopulations of mice and explore the molecular and neural mechanisms underlying individual variability of stress susceptibility (Golden et al., 2011; Higashida et al., 2018; Krishnan et al., 2007; Nie et al., 2018; Shinohara et al., 2018) . In this model, male C57BL/6 and other inbred mice are exposed to attacks from physically dominant and aggressive male CD-1 (ICR) mice for 10 min daily for ten consecutive days. Chronic social defeat stress induces social avoidance in about half of the mice, called susceptible mice, but not in the remaining mice, called resilient mice (Fig. 1A ). In addition to social avoidance, chronic social defeat stress induces behavioral changes similar to depressive symptoms characterized by anhedonia (loss of interest or pleasure), elevated anxiety, sleep and circadian rhythm disturbances, and cognitive dysfunction (Higashida et al., 2018; Krishnan et al., 2007; Nagai et al., 2020) . At least some of these behavioral changes are ameliorated by chronic, but not acute, administration of typical antidepressants (e.g., serotonin reuptake inhibitors) (Berton et al., 2006) , which has provided In addition, immediate early gene (IEG) expressions such as Zif268 and c-Fos in the mPFC are decreased in susceptible mice. The transcription factor ΔFosB is induced in the prelimbic mPFC of susceptible mice after chronic social defeat stress, but in the infralimbic mPFC in resilient mice due to environmental enrichment. The CCK-B receptor is upregulated to mediate the effect of ΔFosB in the prelimbic mPFC for stress susceptibility. Susceptible mice also show a reduction in firing rates of mPFC-projecting VTA dopamine neurons, mPFC dopamine release, and D1 receptor expression in the mPFC. a predictive validity of the model for studying depression pathology. In addition, repetition of social defeat stress is required for behavioral changes as acute social defeat stress (i.e., single exposure to social defeat stress) does not produce significant behavioral deficits such as social avoidance (Shinohara et al., 2018; Tanaka et al., 2012) . Chronic social defeat stress has been shown to alter neuronal morphology in the mPFC (Nie et al., 2018; Shinohara et al., 2018) . Chronic social defeat stress induces dendritic atrophy and decreases dendritic spine density in pyramidal neurons (excitatory, projection neurons) of the mPFC in susceptible mice, but these morphological changes do not occur in resilient mice (Shinohara et al., 2018) . Chronic unpredictable mild stress in rodents reportedly induces similar dendritic atrophy and reduced spine density in mPFC neurons. Thus, morphological changes of mPFC pyramidal neurons are neuronal correlates of chronic stress-induced depressive behaviors (Fig. 1B ). Several studies have reported altered mPFC activity in animal models, showing that molecular correlates of neuronal activity (i.e., immediate early gene expressions such as Zif268 and c-Fos) in the mPFC are decreased in mice susceptible to chronic social defeat stress (Fig. 1B ) (Covington et al., 2010; Nie et al., 2018) . In susceptible mice, optogenetic activation of mPFC neurons during behavioral testing after chronic social defeat stress rapidly reverses depressive behaviors but not elevated anxiety-like behaviors (Covington et al., 2010) . Further, optogenetic stimulation of pyramidal neurons in the infralimbic, but not prelimbic, subregion of the mPFC for 60 min (1 min on and 1 min off for 30 cycles) produces sustained (up to 17 days) antidepressant-like effects in rats (Fuchikami et al., 2015) . These effects are associated with the increased number and function of spine synapses of mPFC layer V pyramidal neurons (Fuchikami et al., 2015) . Environmental enrichment promotes stress resilience in a manner dependent on the infralimbic mPFC with increased expression of the transcription factor ΔFosB (Fig. 1B ) (Lehmann and Herkenham, 2011) , corroborating the importance of the infralimbic mPFC in stress resilience. However, chronic social defeat stress induces ΔFosB in the prelimbic, but not infralimbic, mPFC in susceptible mice, contributing to stress susceptibility by inducing the cholecystokinin (CCK)-B receptor partly (Fig. 1B ) (Vialou et al., 2014) .

llm_chunks.text: portance of the infralimbic mPFC in stress resilience. However, chronic social defeat stress induces ΔFosB in the prelimbic, but not infralimbic, mPFC in susceptible mice, contributing to stress susceptibility by inducing the cholecystokinin (CCK)-B receptor partly (Fig. 1B ) (Vialou et al., 2014) . The distinct roles of the prelimbic and infralimbic mPFC are corroborated by the notion that these subregions oppositely regulate fear and anxiety (Adhikari et al., 2015; Sierra-Mercado et al., 2011) . How these two subregions play different roles in stress susceptibility and resilience awaits future studies. The mPFC likely promotes resilience to chronic stress-induced behavioral changes by its top-down control of several limbic and brainstem targets (Hare and Duman, 2020) . Optogenetic stimulation of mPFC axon terminals within the dorsal raphe nucleus (DRN) decreases chronic social defeat stress-induced social avoidance (Challis et al., 2014) and immobility time in the forced swim test (Warden et al., 2012) . Optogenetic stimulation of mPFC projections to the basolateral amygdala (BLA) or NAc blocks elevated anxiety or social avoidance and anhedonia, respectively, induced by social defeat stress after intra-mPFC CCK infusion (Vialou et al., 2014) . These findings indicate that separate projections from the mPFC to various brain regions are involved in stress resilience in distinct behavioral domains.

llm_chunks.heading: Involvement of dopamine neurons in the ventral tegmental area in stress susceptibility and resilience
llm_chunks.text: Dopamine is a neurotransmitter involved in motor, emotional, and cognitive functions (Nieoullon, 2002) . Dopamine neurons involved in emotional and cognitive functions are located in the ventral tegmental area (VTA) and are composed of several subpopulations, each of which projects to a distinct brain region, including the nucleus accumbens (NAc) and the mPFC (Lammel et al., 2011 (Lammel et al., , 2012)) . Dopamine neurons projecting to the NAc are called the mesoaccumbal dopaminergic pathway and are responsible for motivational behavior through reward and punishment (Lammel et al., 2014) . Dopamine neurons projecting to the mPFC are referred to as the mesoprefrontal dopaminergic pathway and are involved in attention and behavioral flexibility (Floresco, 2013) . A study combining genetic engineering and ex vivo electrophysiology has shown that chronic social defeat stress induces increased firing rates of VTA dopamine neurons with increased I h current (hyperpolarizationactivated cation channel current) in susceptible mice (Krishnan et al., 2007) . This hyperactivity of dopamine neurons results in the release of brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) in the NAc, leading to depressive behaviors after chronic social defeat stress (Krishnan et al., 2007) . In susceptible mice, chronic social defeat stress induces phosphorylation of extracellular signal-regulated kinase (ERK) in dopamine D1 receptor-expressing medium spiny neurons, suggesting that D1-expressing medium spiny neurons are the site of action of BDNF in the NAc after chronic social defeat stress (Wook Koo et al., 2016) . Further studies have supported these findings by showing that VTA dopamine neurons projecting to the NAc display hyperactivity in susceptible mice after chronic social defeat stress and that optogenetically mimicking this hyperactivity of the VTA-NAc dopamine pathway promotes depressive behaviors, including social avoidance and decreased sucrose preference (Chaudhury et al., 2013) . Interestingly, mice resilient to chronic social defeat stress exhibit an even larger I h current in parallel with increased inhibitory potassium currents, suggesting homeostatic excitatory/inhibitory current balance maintaining stable normal firing of these neurons in resilient mice (Friedman et al., 2014) . Emerging evidence has revealed noradrenergic regulation of VTA dopamine neurons in stress resilience. Locus coeruleus (LC) noradrenergic neurons projecting to the VTA exhibit enhanced firing rates in resilient but not susceptible mice (Zhang et al., 2019) . Consistently, resilient mice exhibit higher noradrenaline levels in the VTA than susceptible mice (Isingrini et al., 2016) . Repeated optogenetic stimulation of LC noradrenergic neurons projecting to the VTA (20 min per day for 10 days) in susceptible mice suppresses the hyperactivity of VTA dopamine neurons and reverses depressive behaviors in a manner dependent on α1 and β3 adrenergic receptors in the VTA (Zhang et al., 2019) . These findings suggest the role of LC noradrenergic neurons in promoting stress resilience via VTA dopamine neurons.

llm_chunks.heading: Involvement of prefrontal dopaminergic system in stress resilience
llm_chunks.text: Studies using chronic social defeat stress have revealed a crucial role of the prefrontal dopaminergic system in stress resilience. In contrast to VTA-NAc dopamine neurons, VTA dopamine neurons projecting to the mPFC exhibit hypoactivity in susceptible mice, and optogenetic inhibition of the VTA-mPFC dopamine pathway induces social avoidance (Chaudhury et al., 2013) . These findings suggest that the VTA-NAc and VTA-mPFC dopamine pathways are functionally distinct in mediating stress susceptibility and resilience, respectively. Dopamine neurons projecting to the mPFC are preferentially activated by stressful stimuli, such as electric shock (Roth et al., 1988) . However, it remained unclear whether the dopaminergic response in the mPFC is involved in stress-induced behavioral changes. Acute social defeat stress, which does not induce depressive behaviors, activates VTA dopamine neurons and enhances dopamine metabolic turnover (a biochemical index of dopamine release) in the mPFC (Fig. 1B ) (Tanaka et al., 2012) . While acute social defeat stress prominently induces prefrontal dopamine response and dopamine D1 receptor signaling in prefrontal excitatory neurons, chronic social defeat stress attenuates this dopamine response and reduces the expression of dopamine D1 receptors in the mPFC of susceptible mice (Fig. 1B ) (Shinohara et al., 2018; Tanaka et al., 2012) . Pharmacological ablation of dopaminergic projections to the mPFC or knockdown of dopamine D1 receptors in mPFC excitatory neurons facilitates chronic social defeat stress-induced social avoidance (Shinohara et al., 2018; Tanaka et al., 2012) . Notably, acute social defeat stress does not usually induce social avoidance, but it does in mice with these dopaminergic manipulations. Stress-induced D1 receptor signaling increases arborization and spines of apical dendrites of mPFC layer II/III pyramidal neurons (Shinohara et al., 2018) , which could be a novel neuronal correlate of stress resilience (Fig. 2 ). Further, acute social defeat stress induces neural activity in the interstitial nucleus of the posterior limb of the anterior commissure (IPAC), a subregion of the extended amygdala (Shammah-Lagnado et al., 2001) , in a manner dependent on D1 receptors in the mPFC (Fig. 2 ) (Numa et al., 2019) . These findings collectively suggest that D1 receptor signaling of mPFC neurons upon acute social defeat stress contributes to inducing dendritic growth of these neurons and activating the extended amygdala, leading to stress resilience, and that this mechanism is attenuated with repetition of stress (Fig. 2 ). However, the D1 receptor signaling to mediate stress resilience is unclear, and the causal link between the dendritic growth and stress resilience also remains to be investigated. As there are many D2 receptor-expressing neurons in the mPFC, they could be involved in stress resilience. Indeed, behaviorally locked optogenetic stimulation of D2 receptor-expressing mPFC neurons increases effortful responses to tail suspension stress, and D2 receptor knockdown in mPFC neurons shortens individual episodes of the effortful responses (Wilke et al., 2022) . Thus, D2 receptor-expressing mPFC neurons, as well as D2 receptors, could suppress depressive behavior and cooperate with D1 receptor-expressing mPFC neurons as well as D1 receptors for stress resilience. D1 receptors and D2 receptors are expressed in different populations of mPFC neurons that largely correspond to intratelencephalic (IT) cortical neurons and pyramidal tract (PT) cortical neurons, respectively. These neuronal populations have different projection targets and morphological, electrophysiological, and pharmacological characteristics (Dembrow and Johnston, 2014) , suggesting that D1 receptor-expressing mPFC neurons and D2 receptor-expressing mPFC neurons may function differently. However, the functional roles of the respective neuronal populations and their projections to other brain structures in stress resilience remain to be fully elucidated.

llm_chunks.heading: Dopamine-mediated potentiation of glutamatergic transmission in the prefrontal cortex for sustained antidepressant actions of acute ketamine treatment
llm_chunks.text: The serendipitous discovery of the rapid and sustained antidepressant actions of low-dose ketamine in MDD patients (Berman et al., 2000; Zarate et al., 2006) provided a conceptual impact on the treatment of depression (Krystal et al., 2019) . Then, rodent studies have identified multiple neural mechanisms underlying antidepressant actions of acute ketamine treatment. Low-dose ketamine exerts rapid and sustained antidepressant actions, and these two components with different time courses are thought to be mediated by distinct brain regions. Rodent studies have shown that the activation of mPFC pyramidal neurons is required to produce sustained antidepressant-like actions of acute ketamine treatment (Duman et al., 2016; Gould et al., 2019) . Although ketamine is an N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) receptor antagonist developed as a dissociative anesthetic, low-dose ketamine administration paradoxically produces a rapid but transient increase in extracellular glutamate levels in the mPFC of rodents (Chowdhury et al., 2017; Moghaddam et al., 1997) via inhibiting NMDA receptors on inhibitory interneurons (Ali et al., 2020; Gerhard et al., 2020; Homayoun and Moghaddam, 2007; Widman and McMahon, 2018) . This glutamate burst is thought to induce dendritic spine formation and synaptic activity on mPFC pyramidal neurons at least at 24 h or later (Li et al., 2010) . A recent study using a photoactivatable probe that can selectively reverse activity-dependent spine formation demonstrates the necessity of ketamine-induced spine formation in the mPFC for the sustained antidepressant-like effects (Fig. 2 ) (Moda-Sava et al., 2019) . Pharmacological studies in rodents indicate that brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) release and mechanistic target of the rapamycin complex 1 (mTORC1) signaling are involved in the effects of low-dose ketamine in inducing spine formation in the mPFC and its sustained antidepressant-like actions (Lepack et al., 2014; Li et al., 2010 Li et al., , 2011;; Liu et al., 2012) . In humans, although low-dose ketamine increased the glutamate content in the prefrontal cortex within a few hours (Abdallah et al., 2017 (Abdallah et al., , 2018)) , systemic administration of rapamycin, an mTORC1 inhibitor, failed to block but prolonged ketamine's antidepressant Fig. 2 . Hypothetical roles of prefrontal D1 receptors in stress resilience and sustained antidepressant responses. Acute stress and ketamine promote not only glutamate release but also dopamine release in the mPFC that activates dopamine D1 receptors on excitatory neurons. This dopamine D1 receptor signaling contributes to increasing dendritic growth (e.g., dendritic arborization and spine formation) of these neurons and affects the activity of downstream structures, namely the basolateral amygdala, BNST, and IPAC. These neural circuits are proposed to underlie stress resilience and rapid antidepressant responses by suppressing depressive behaviors. effects in MDD patients (Abdallah et al., 2020) . This apparent discrepancy from rodent findings has been interpreted that, in rodents, rapamycin was injected into the mPFC to block the sustained antidepressant-like actions of ketamine (Li et al., 2010) , although this interpretation remains to be proven. Interestingly, ketamine blocks NMDA receptors on glutamatergic neurons in the hippocampus and the lateral habenula for its rapid antidepressant-like actions (Autry et al., 2011; Lin et al., 2021; Yang et al., 2018) . In the hippocampus, BDNF, but not mTORC1 signaling, is involved in the rapid antidepressant-like actions. NMDA receptor blockade at rest in hippocampal pyramidal neurons reportedly increases BDNF protein translation for the rapid antidepressant-like actions (Autry et al., 2011) . Thus, BDNF and its downstream consequences may be involved in the induction and maintenance of ketamine's antidepressant actions via different molecular and cellular mechanisms. In addition to ketamine's effects on glutamate neurotransmission, low-dose ketamine stimulates VTA dopamine neurons and produces a rapid and transient increase in extracellular levels of dopamine in the mPFC (Moghaddam et al., 1997; Witkin et al., 2016) . Since other NMDA receptor blockers, MK-801 and phencyclidine, also stimulate dopamine release in the mPFC and nucleus accumbens (Schmidt and Fadayel, 1996; Takahata and Moghaddam, 2003) , NMDA receptor antagonism is likely involved in the dopaminergic effects of low-dose ketamine. Although the rapid antidepressant effects of D1 receptor agonists have not been examined in MDD patients due to their possible side effects, the infusion of a D1 receptor agonist, SKF81297, into the rodent mPFC produces sustained antidepressant-like effects similar to ketamine, and a prior infusion of a D1 receptor antagonist, SCH39166, into the rodent mPFC blocks the sustained antidepressant-like responses to acute ketamine treatment (Hare et al., 2019) . Consistently, the knockdown of D1 receptors in mPFC excitatory neurons abolishes the sustained antidepressant-like behavioral actions of ketamine (Pothula et al., 2020) . These findings indicate the roles of prefrontal D1 receptors for the sustained antidepressant-like actions of ketamine, although their involvement in the rapid antidepressant-like actions remains to be investigated. Rodent studies report that acute stress rapidly and simultaneously promotes glutamate and dopamine release in the mPFC (Popoli et al., 2011; Tanaka et al., 2012) , and these neurotransmitters have been shown to interact with each other in the mPFC. Activation of D1 receptors increases the excitability of mPFC pyramidal neurons (Lavin and Grace, 2001) and their surface expression of NMDA receptors and AMPA receptors (Gao and Wolf, 2008; Sun et al., 2005) and excitatory synaptic inputs (Bjorkholm et al., 2017; Gonzalez-Islas and Hablitz, 2003; Gurden et al., 2000) .

llm_chunks.text: ptors increases the excitability of mPFC pyramidal neurons (Lavin and Grace, 2001) and their surface expression of NMDA receptors and AMPA receptors (Gao and Wolf, 2008; Sun et al., 2005) and excitatory synaptic inputs (Bjorkholm et al., 2017; Gonzalez-Islas and Hablitz, 2003; Gurden et al., 2000) . In addition, in mPFC slices, a heteromeric D1 receptor/NMDA receptor complex has been suggested to modulate NMDA receptor functions (Missale et al., 2006; Sarantis et al., 2009) . Since D1 receptor signaling contributes to acute stress-induced dendritic growth in the mPFC, it could augment glutamatergic transmission in the long term. These mechanisms have been postulated to allow prefrontal D1 receptors to potentiate glutamatergic transmission for the sustained antidepressant-like actions of low-dose ketamine (Hare et al., 2019; Pothula et al., 2020) , although the involvement of each mechanism remains to be tested.

llm_chunks.heading: Prefrontal circuitry mediating sustained antidepressant actions of acute ketamine treatment
llm_chunks.text: Rodent studies have begun to reveal neural circuits underlying sustained antidepressant-like actions of acute ketamine treatment. The requirement of D1 receptor signaling in the mPFC for the actions of ketamine led us to explore the role of neural circuits originating from D1 receptor-expressing mPFC neurons. Hare et al. demonstrate that the optogenetic activation of D1 receptor-expressing, but not D2 receptorexpressing, mPFC neurons reproduces sustained antidepressant-like responses similar to ketamine at 24 h and at least up to a week. In addition, optogenetic or chemogenetic inhibition of D1 receptor-expressing, but not D2 receptor-expressing, mPFC neurons concomitant with systemic ketamine administration blocks antidepressant-like effects of ketamine at 24 h and later (Hare et al., 2019) . Optogenetic activation of mPFC neurons expressing D1 receptors, but not D2 receptors, induces c-Fos expression in the basolateral amygdala (BLA) and bed nucleus of the stria terminalis (BNST) (Hare et al., 2019) . Optogenetic and chemogenetic studies indicate that D1 receptor-expressing mPFC neurons activate BLA to reduce passive coping (immobility time) in the forced swim test, whereas these neurons do BNST for antidepressant-like effects on anxiety-like and reward-seeking behaviors, measured in the novelty suppressed feeding test and female urine sniffing test, respectively (Shinohara et al., 2019) . These findings suggest that distinct targets downstream of D1 receptor-expressing mPFC neurons contribute to sustained antidepressant responses to acute ketamine treatment in different behavioral domains (Fig. 2 ). Although it was reported that optogenetic stimulation of D2 receptor-expressing mPFC neurons produced antidepressant-like effects (Wilke et al., 2022) , the stimulation was applied during but not 24 h before behavioral testing. These findings suggest that D1 receptor-expressing and D2 receptor-expressing mPFC neurons may contribute to the induction and expression of sustained antidepressant actions of acute ketamine treatment. Unlike D1 receptor-expressing mPFC neurons, the efferent projections of D2 receptor-expressing mPFC neurons that mediate the sustained antidepressant actions have not been studied. As described above, D1 receptor-expressing and D2 receptor-expressing mPFC neurons are separate populations of excitatory neurons with different projection targets (Dembrow and Johnston, 2014; Gee et al., 2012) . Thus, distinct neural circuits activated by the respective neuronal populations could be involved in the induction/maintenance of the sustained antidepressant actions and their behavioral expression. This possibility warrants future investigation. Besides mPFC efferents described above, rodent studies have begun to identify mPFC afferents underlying antidepressant-like responses. Optogenetic inhibition of the ventral hippocampus-to-mPFC pathway blocks the antidepressant-like effects of ketamine (Carreno et al., 2016) . However, it remains unclear whether this pathway is involved in the immediate action of ketamine as this effect was tested only when the inhibition was conducted during the behavioral testing, but not at the time of ketamine administration. A recent study shows that mGluR2/3 negative allosteric modulators (NAMs) enhance glutamatergic transmission from the mediodorsal thalamus to the mPFC and produce antidepressant-like effects on passive coping and reward-seeking behavior (Joffe et al., 2020) . Chemogenetic inhibition of this glutamatergic pathway concomitant with the administration of mGluR2/3 NAMs prevents their antidepressant-like effects (Joffe et al., 2020) . Further studies are needed to examine whether this glutamatergic pathway is involved in the antidepressant-like actions of ketamine.

llm_chunks.heading: Conclusion
llm_chunks.text: As described in this review article, preclinical studies in animal models have identified the formation and potentiation of spine synapses of mPFC excitatory neurons as key mediators in producing sustained antidepressant responses to acute ketamine treatment. Acute stress also induces dendritic growth, including dendritic arborization and spine formation, concomitant with stress resilience. D1 receptors in prefrontal neurons are involved in both stress resilience and the sustained antidepressant responses. Further neural-circuit analyses revealed that D1 receptor-expressing mPFC neurons mediate both stress resilience and the sustained antidepressant effects via their projection to the extended amygdala. These findings led us to speculate a common mechanism underlying stress resilience and the sustained antidepressant effects. However, the D1 receptor signaling and its cellular actions are unclear, and the causal role of acute stress-induced dendritic growth in stress resilience is unknown. Therefore, more studies are needed to understand the mechanisms of D1 receptor action in both of these effects, which might help bridge the gap between stress resilience and antidepressant actions. There remain several questions to solve to substantiate the link between stress resilience and the antidepressant effects. So far, the roles of prefrontal D1 receptors have been shown only for resilience-promoting neural circuits activated upon social defeat stress. Stress resilience can be promoted by various conditions, including environmental enrichment during postnatal development, mild exercise, and dietary intake of ω3 polyunsaturated fatty acids. It has not been examined whether and how prefrontal D1 receptors and mPFC neurons expressing them are involved in these resilience-promoting conditions. Given that the rapid and sustained antidepressant actions of ketamine appear to utilize different molecular and cellular mechanisms, whether the neural mechanisms of stress resilience by prefrontal D1 receptors are related to the rapid antidepressant actions remains elusive. It should be noted that the neural mechanisms of the antidepressant actions of low-dose ketamine have mostly been analyzed with its acute treatment. Thus, whether the prefrontal D1 receptor-mediated mechanism is also executed with chronic low-dose ketamine treatment also needs to be examined. Since some individuals who do not respond to conventional antidepressants, such as selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, can be treated by lowdose ketamine, whether stress resilience is selectively involved in the ketamine's effects or, more broadly, in multiple antidepressant actions needs to be tested. Nonetheless, prefrontal D1 receptors and mPFC neurons expressing them play pivotal roles in stress resilience and the sustained antidepressant actions of ketamine at least in part. Regarding the roles of D1 receptor-expressing mPFC neurons, how their afferents and efferents orchestrate whole-brain activities and how emotional and cognitive processing is affected to confer stress resilience and the sustained antidepressant responses remain unknown. Whether the neural circuits serving stress resilience and the sustained antidepressant responses have unique molecular and cellular signatures also remains unknown. For these questions, cutting-edge technologies such as in vivo two-photon microscopy, multielectrode electrophysiology, and single-cell multi-omics should be used in combination. Another important question on stress resilience is how its individual variability arises. Early-life adversity is thought to result in life-long vulnerability to stress, an increased risk of MDD, and decreased response and remission rate after antidepressant therapy (Davidson and McEwen, 2012; Nanni et al., 2012; Tost et al., 2015; Williams et al., 2016) . How early-life stress affects neurodevelopmental trajectories of resilience-related neural circuits, leading to individual variability of resilience, warrants future investigation. Understanding these unanswered questions on stress resilience will provide essential information exploitable for developing novel therapeutics by pharmacologically targeting or directly manipulating (via transcranial magnetic stimulation or deep brain stimulation) neurobiological mechanisms of stress resilience and their neurodevelopmental trajectories.

Prepulse inhibition (PPI) is a behavioural measure of sensorimotor gating that is disrupted in schizophrenia. We tested the ability for antipsychotic drugs with diverse pharmacological actions to (1) ameliorate NMDAr antagonist-induced disruptions to gamma oscillations and (2) attenuate NMDAr antagonist-induced disruptions to PPI. We hypothesized that antipsychotic-mediated improvement of PPI deficits would be accompanied by a normalization of gamma oscillatory activity. Wistar rats were implanted with extradural electrodes to facilitate recording of electroencephalogram during PPI behavioural testing. In each session, the rats were administered haloperidol (0.25 mg kg(-1)), clozapine (5 mg kg(-1)), olanzapine (5 mg kg(-1)), LY379268 (3 mg kg(-1)), NFPS (sarcosine, 1 mg kg(-1)), d-serine (1800 mg kg(-1)) or vehicle, followed by the NMDAr antagonists MK-801(0.16 mg kg(-1)), ketamine (5 mg kg(-1)) or vehicle. Outcome measures were auditory-evoked, as well as ongoing, gamma oscillations and PPI. Although treatment with all the clinically validated antipsychotic drugs reduced ongoing gamma oscillations, clozapine was the only compound that prevented the sensory-evoked gamma deficit produced by ketamine and MK-801. In addition, clozapine was also the only antipsychotic that attenuated the disruption to PPI produced by the NMDAr antagonists. We conclude that disruptions to evoked, but not ongoing, gamma oscillations caused by NMDAr antagonists are functionally relevant, and suggest that compounds, which restore sensory-evoked gamma oscillations may improve sensory processing in patients with schizophrenia.
